question: What does 'venue' mean on a notarial certificate?

options.text: The place where the notarial act was performed
options.why: Correct. On a certificate, venue is the state and county where the notarial act took place.

options.text: The court where a case is heard
options.why: Wrong. In litigation 'venue' can mean the court's location, but on a certificate it means the place of the act.
Wrong. The notary's residence has nothing to do with venue.
Wrong. Venue is about place, not the subject of the document.

explanation: Venue identifies where the notarization took place.

refs.title: Definitions: Venue (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 22)

question: What does 'ss.' (scilicet) mean in a venue?

options.why: Correct. 'Ss.' abbreviates scilicet, Latin for 'namely' or 'in particular'.
Wrong. A common guess, but 'ss.' doesn't stand for 'signed and sealed'.
Wrong. 'Ss.' doesn't stand for 'sworn statement'.
Wrong. It has nothing to do with Social Security.

explanation: 'Ss.' stands for scilicet, meaning 'namely' or 'in particular'.

refs.title: Definitions: Venue (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 22)

question: What is a 'grantor'?

options.why: Correct. The grantor conveys (transfers) property; the grantee receives it.
Wrong. The person who receives property is the grantee.
Wrong. The notary is an impartial officer, never the grantor.
Wrong. A lender under a mortgage is the mortgagee, not the grantor.

explanation: A grantor conveys property to a grantee.

refs.title: Definitions: Conveyance (Deed) (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is a 'testator'?

options.text: A person who makes a will
options.why: Correct. A testator is a person who makes a will.

options.text: A person who takes a test
options.why: Wrong. In law, 'testator' refers to making a will, not taking a test.
Wrong. A witness in a deposition is a deponent or witness, not a testator.
Wrong. An executor carries out the will; the testator makes it.

explanation: A testator is a person who makes a will.

refs.title: Definitions: Will (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 22)

question: What is 'protest' in the notary context?

options.text: A formal statement that a negotiable instrument was presented and dishonored (not paid or accepted)
options.why: Correct. A protest is a formal certificate that a negotiable instrument was presented and dishonored (not paid or accepted); notaries may make protests.
Wrong. In notary law, 'protest' isn't a public demonstration.
Wrong. An objection in court is a different use of the word.
Wrong. A complaint against a notary isn't what 'protest' means here.

explanation: A protest certifies that a negotiable instrument was presented for payment or acceptance and was refused.
source: N.Y. Exec. Law §135; NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Protest)

refs.title: Definitions: Protest (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)
N.Y. Exec. Law §135 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)

question: What is a 'power of attorney'?

options.text: A written document authorizing one person to act as another's agent
options.why: Correct. A power of attorney authorizes an agent (the attorney-in-fact) to act for the principal.
Wrong. A lawyer's license is unrelated to a power of attorney.
Wrong. A power of attorney is granted by the principal, not ordered by a court.
Wrong. The notary's commission isn't a power of attorney.

explanation: A power of attorney authorizes an agent (attorney-in-fact) to act for the principal.

refs.title: Definitions: Power of Attorney (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: What is 'duress'?

options.text: Unlawful pressure or threats that force someone to act against their will
options.why: Correct. Duress is unlawful pressure or threats forcing someone to act against their will; a notary shouldn't proceed if a signer is under duress.
Wrong. Duress has nothing to do with due dates.
Wrong. Duress isn't a kind of seal.
Wrong. Duress isn't a fee.

explanation: Duress is compulsion by threat or force; an act done under duress isn't voluntary.

refs.title: Definitions: Duress (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is a 'lessee'?

options.text: A tenant who rents property under a lease
options.why: Correct. The lessee is the tenant who rents under a lease.
Wrong. The landlord is the lessor.
Wrong. A lender is a mortgagee or creditor, not a lessee.
Wrong. 'Lessee' has nothing to do with notary staff.

explanation: A lessee is the tenant in a lease; the lessor is the owner.

refs.title: Definitions: Lease (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: What is a 'lien'?

options.text: A legal right or claim against property as security for a debt
options.why: Correct. A lien is a legal claim against property securing a debt, such as a mortgage or judgment lien.
Wrong. A notarial certificate records a notarial act; it isn't a claim on property.
Wrong. An affidavit is a sworn statement, not a claim on property.
Wrong. Transferring a deed is a conveyance, not a lien.

explanation: A lien is a claim on property securing a debt or obligation.

refs.title: Definitions: Lien (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: What does 'ex parte' mean?

options.text: On behalf of, or by, one party only, without the other party present
options.why: Correct. Ex parte means by or for one party only, without the other side present.
Wrong. 'Outside the state' isn't what ex parte means.
Wrong. 'After the fact' is ex post facto, a different term.
Wrong. Ex parte has nothing to do with fees.

explanation: Ex parte means by or for one party only.

refs.title: Definitions: Ex Parte (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is 'real property'?

options.text: Land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings
options.why: Correct. Real property is land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings.
Wrong. 'Any valuable item' is too broad; movable items are personal property.
Wrong. Cash and bank accounts are personal property.
Wrong. Cars and furniture are chattels (personal property).

explanation: Real property is land and things permanently attached to it.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §290 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: What is a 'chattel'?

options.text: Personal property, such as goods or furniture
options.why: Correct. A chattel is movable personal property, such as goods or furniture.
Wrong. Land is real property, the opposite of a chattel.
Wrong. A deed is an instrument conveying real property, not a chattel.
Wrong. A court officer is a person, not property.

explanation: A chattel is personal property, as opposed to real property.

refs.title: Definitions: Chattel (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is a 'subordination clause'?

options.text: A clause that ranks a lien or mortgage below another
options.why: Correct. A subordination clause makes one lien or mortgage junior to another, changing their priority.

options.text: A clause making the notary subordinate to the clerk
options.why: Wrong. It has nothing to do with the relationship between notaries and clerks.
Wrong. It doesn't require a witness.
Wrong. Cancelling a deed is rescission or revocation, not subordination.

explanation: A subordination clause makes one interest (often a mortgage) junior to another.

refs.title: Definitions: Subordination Clause (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 22)

question: What does it mean to 'attest'?

options.text: To witness the execution of a document and sign as a witness
options.why: Correct. To attest is to witness the execution of a document and sign as a witness.
Wrong. In law, attest doesn't mean taking a test.
Wrong. Attesting is the opposite of refusing; it confirms execution.
Wrong. Recording a deed is done by the county clerk, not by attesting.

explanation: To attest is to witness execution and sign as a witness.

refs.title: Definitions: Attest (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is a 'contract'?

options.text: An agreement between competent parties, for consideration, to do or not do something lawful
options.why: Correct. A contract is an agreement between competent parties, for consideration, to do or not do something lawful.
Wrong. Many notarized documents, such as affidavits, aren't contracts.
Wrong. A promise without consideration generally isn't an enforceable contract.
Wrong. A judgment is a court's decision, not an agreement.

explanation: A contract is an agreement between competent parties, for consideration, to do or refrain from doing a lawful act.

refs.title: Definitions: Contract (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is an 'executor'?

options.text: A person named in a will to carry out its provisions
options.why: Correct. An executor is named in a will to carry out its provisions.

options.text: The person who signs a deed
options.why: Wrong. The person who signs a deed is the grantor or signer, not an executor.
Wrong. 'Executor' doesn't mean a notary who executes certificates.
Wrong. A court clerk is a court officer, not an executor.

explanation: An executor is named in a will to carry out its terms; an administrator is appointed when there is no named executor.

refs.title: Definitions: Executor (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)
Definitions: Administrator (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
